parsed.study_design: Mixed-methods ethnographic panel study and randomized-sample economic experiments
parsed.population_and_sample: Households in Villa Israel, a water-scarce squatter settlement in Cochabamba; ethnographic interviews with 101 household heads from 72 randomly sampled households, plus economic experiments with 67 randomly sampled residents.
parsed.exposure: Religiosity and Christian norms of charity, including church-attendance frequency and relationships with family members, coreligionists, and neighbors as informal institutional influences on water sharing.
parsed.outcome: Household water sharing and receipt, generosity, and enforcement of fair-giving norms that facilitate access to drinking water during shortages.
parsed.rationale: The Setting and Methods sections (pp. 312–317) identify a population lacking municipal water service and describe 18 months of ethnography, repeated household interviews, and economic experiments. The Qualitative Results report observed household water giving and receipt (p. 317 onward), while the Discussion and Conclusions (pp. 332–335) identify Christian charity norms and religiosity as an informal institutional mechanism facilitating water sharing and access.
